description: A line-sequential file in ASCII whose records end with 0x0A, which is the delimited file an adopter on Linux is likeliest to hand the tool first. Under the terminator placement a delimiter follows every record, the last included, so three records carry three of them. Two of the three hold a binary count whose own bytes are 0x0A -- a PIC S9(4) COMP item holding 10 is 00 0A and one holding 2570 is 0A 0A -- so a consumer that searched the input for the delimiter would cut the first record after five bytes and the second after four and again after five. A consumer that counts the extent reads them as the numbers they are. The third record's count is zero, so its bytes carry no 0x0A at all and it is the ordinary record the other two are read against.
source: docs/ir/SPEC.md, "Four framings, and none of them is a RECFM", "The extent governs, and framing is checked against it", "A delimiter is bytes, not a character" and "Terminator, separator, and the last record"; docs/layout/SPEC.md, "Physical framing" and "A delimiter is bytes, and it has a placement", which is where 0x0A is named as what the same file ends its records with once it has moved to Linux; the binary count is cobol-go codec/SPEC.md Appendix A.5's encoding, and the rule the record is aimed at is the one "The extent governs, and framing is checked against it" carries, that a consumer MUST NOT find a record's end by searching for a delimiter
